entries.title: Chinatown and Bridgeport residents press Amtrak leaders to 'pump the breaks' on rail yard plan
entries.summary: <p>Amtrak officials and developers faced off against angry community members Thursday, opposing construction plans for a massive rail yard in Chinatown, Bridgeport and Armour Square beginning as early as the end of this year.</p><p>The plan, headed by White Sox minority owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" target="_blank" >Justin Ishbia’s</a> company, Canal Edge LLC, includes a proposal for the Sox to play at a mixed-use facility along the Chicago River called The Railyards in the South Loop and Amtrak’s maintenance facility to move into the neighborhood on South Canal Street between West 33rd and 35th streets.</p><p>Hundreds of residents, some dressed in T-shirts that read “Protect our community, stop Amtrak’s rail yard,” flooded the meeting. Tensions rose as Amtrak leaders and developers claimed there were no significant impacts on the environment or quality of life for nearby residents housed near the proposed site.</p><p>Residents responded by questioning the studies Amtrak has done regarding impacts on safety, the environment, noise and other factors. The project has received $600 million and a categorical exclusion from the federal government to bypass certain environmental tests and an environmental impact statement to break ground faster, but residents also questioned that.</p><p>“You’re treating us like we’re idiots. We’re not idiots,” one resident said. “We’re intelligent, hardworking people making our home here.”</p><p>Steven Segerlin, who runs commercial development at Amtrak, said the company needs a new site for a rail yard to replace its current 14th Street facility. The revamped site would allow the company to modernize its maintenance, cleaning and storage practices, allowing for fewer delays.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Lincoln-Way board votes to allow students involved in racist incident to withdraw instead of being expelled
entries.summary: <p>The Lincoln-Way School District Board of Education voted unanimously to allow the students involved in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/05/lincoln-way-east-homewood-flossmoor-racial-harassment" >racial harassment incident</a> during the football game at Homewood-Flossmoor on Sept. 4 to withdraw voluntarily from Lincoln-Way East rather than be expelled.</p><p>“This investigation, which involved interviewing numerous students, reviewing multiple video recordings and angles, and speaking with their attorneys, took the administration only eight school days and ultimately resulted in the administration recommending expulsion for the students determined to have been involved,” Supt. Scott Tingley said at the school board meeting on Thursday. “The parents of those students have chosen, however, to voluntarily withdraw their children from Lincoln-Way East High School and forfeit all student privileges rather than proceed with the expulsion process.”</p><p>The Lincoln-Way East students were caught on video racially taunting H-F students at a football game in Flossmoor by mimicking monkeys.</p><p>The school board did not name the students or specifically outline the reasons for each student’s discipline. The board returned from closed session and voted to allow six students to withdraw instead of being expelled. Tingley spoke after the vote.</p><p>“My responsibility as superintendent was to ensure the law and the board of education policies were followed at every step with respect to those students’ discipline,” Tingley said. “To do that, the administration conducted a thorough and timely investigation and assessed each student’s individual level of involvement and offered every one of them the right to be heard.”</p><p>The Lincoln-Way school board acknowledged what happened at the football game and released an apology statement the next day. </p><p>Later the same weekend, Homewood-Flossmoor officials accused a Lincoln-Way East girls cross-country coach and team members of racial abuse at a cross country meet in Western Springs.</p><p>H-F provided written statements from three cross-country athletes describing a Lincoln-Way East coach making comments about “running past those monkeys,” and that some of the Lincoln-Way East team began cheering and making “noises that were racist” and “monkey gestures.”</p><p>Lincoln-Way investigated the incident and concluded that “neither its staff nor student athletes intended to harass, intimidate or offend any of their competitors or those competitors’ families.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-sports/2026/09/09/lincoln-way-east-homewood-flossmoor-racisim-jennifer-norrell" >After alleged racism, Homewood-Flossmoor weighs future with Lincoln-Way East</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Tingley addressed the cross-country incident at Thursday’s board meeting.</p><p>“The district and certain of its employees have been threatened with legal action, and the allegations surrounding that incident are currently under investigation by the [Illinois High School Association],” Tingley said. “We are fully cooperating with the IHSA and will cooperate with any other appropriate agency or law enforcement authority should an additional investigation occur.</p><p>“While that investigation remains ongoing, I will not make additional public comments regarding the allegations. The district has already made one public statement available noting that it has been unable to corroborate the allegations.</p><p>“Once the IHSA has completed its investigation and it is clear that no additional investigations are pending, I intend to address the matter more fully.”</p><p>The IHSA's Matt Troha told the Sun-Times earlier on Thursday that the action at the Lincoln-Way school board meeting would "provide the IHSA with a better timeline moving forward."<br></p>

entries.title: Miguel Vargas, White Sox, don't mind playing from behind: 'We like being the underdog'
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox returned home this week, in second place in the division standings for the first time since beating the Guardians on Independence Day.</p><p>Maybe it’s for the best.</p><p>“We play better when we’re behind,” All-Star third baseman <b>Miguel Vargas</b> told the Sun-Times. “We like being the underdog. We like to go out there when people do not believe in us.”</p><p>Beginning his career with the Dodgers, bouncing between Triple-A and the majors, Vargas has been on hand for a post-clinch locker room celebration in the major leagues before. Now, as the heart and soul of a Sox lineup fighting to stay afloat in the American League Central, he thinks champagne would taste sweeter in the White Sox clubhouse.</p><p>“With the Dodgers, you always expect to go to the World Series every year,” Vargas said. “When you don’t do it, it’s a failure. Here, I feel nobody believes in us. Everyone doubts us. We were supposed to be the 28th team in MLB this year [according to] ESPN. Now we’re on the way to the postseason, and being underdogs is what it’s about. I feel like that’s what makes us better, being underdogs. That’s what’s brought us to this beautiful year we’ve had.”</p><p>Recent weeks have found the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/13/this-is-why-you-play-white-sox-readying-for-all-important-al-central-showdown-in-cleveland-will-venable-davis-martin-sean-burke-colson-montgomery-randal-grichuk" target="_blank" ><u>Sox trying to reclaim the loose clubhouse atmosphere</u></a> they had while defying expectations, like the ones Vargas referenced, with a 50-45 first half mark. Now that a crushing series loss in Cleveland has their division title odds looking shaky again, maybe they should embrace that feeling.</p><p>“We put ourselves in this position, and we need to clean it up,” Vargas said. “We’re going to be there in the playoffs, and kick some ass too.”</p><p><b>Help from the other side</b></p><p>After <b>Sean Burke</b> gave up a career-worst seven runs in just 1 ⅓ innings on Sept. 8 against Pittsburgh, he sought insight from a surprising source: the opposing No. 2 hitter from that night.</p><p>“I work out with <b>Brandon Lowe</b> in the offseason with my agency,” said Burke, who is a Bledsoe Agency client alongside the Pirates infielder. “So I was talking to him a little bit about what he was seeing, how he felt in the box based on prior times he’s faced me.”</p><p>Lowe’s observations that Burke’s pitches were cutting and blending together lined up with what he was already working on. Ahead of recovering for five innings without an earned run allowed on Monday in Cleveland, Burke focused on correcting his stride direction, and restoring the feeling behind the baseball upon release.</p><p>Lowe is a pending free agent, so he had little reason not to help out a friend.</p><p><b>Montgomery is day-to-day</b></p><p>After leaving Wednesday’s game with a left wrist contusion caused by a hit-by-pitch, <b>Colson Montgomery</b> was out of the lineup Thursday. The Sox say Montgomery is day-to-day, but that day is unlikely to be Friday.</p><p>“There’s still a lot of pain involved in him swinging,” said manager <b>Will Venable</b>.</p><p><b>Castillo to the bullpen</b></p><p>With his 7.76 ERA in a White Sox uniform and nine games remaining, the team is abandoning the idea of trade-deadline acquisition <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/11/white-sox-starter-luis-castillo-feels-hes-very-very-close-to-righting-ship-after-working-on-mechanics-colson-montgomery-strikeout-record-chase-meidroth-joey-bart-will-venable" target="_blank" ><b><u>Luis Castillo</u></b><u> providing a boost to the rotation</u></a>. Venable said Castillo’s next appearance will be out of the bullpen, and Friday’s scheduled starter <b>David Sandlin </b>is effectively <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/15/a-new-and-improved-david-sandlin-should-have-staying-power-in-white-sox-rotation-noah-schultz-colson-montgomery-will-venable-brian-bannister-jose-urquidy" target="_blank" ><u>taking his spot in the rotation</u></a>.</p>

entries.title: Tim Anderson grateful, at peace in retirement as White Sox honor the two-time All-Star's career
entries.summary: <p>Thursday’s retirement ceremony for<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/10/tim-anderson-retirement-chicago-white-sox-southside-city-connect-uniforms-field-of-dreams-game" target="_blank" ><u> former two-time All-Star Tim Anderson</u></a> felt sudden, even with advanced notice.</p><p>“He feels like the story of why Major League Baseball players try to get what they can get when they can get it, because it happens so fast,” said former Sox announcer Jason Benetti, in town to call the game for the Tigers. “His story is some of the brightest lightning in the largest bottle for a time. And then suddenly it's gone.”</p><p>The highlights of Anderson played on the Rate Field Jumbotron were of pristine video quality. The old Southside City Connect jerseys the team played in triggered a nostalgia for an era where Anderson was the heartbeat of the franchise, but were in use in 2024. Just before Anderson was bathed in applause by a thankful crowd, he was congratulated by Tommy Pham–five years his senior–before the Sox DH continued on to his pregame warmups.</p><p>Reached for comment, former White Sox general manager Rick Hahn recalled an anecdote that feels ancient–Anderson convincing him to approve Team USA playing him at second base, and keying a mercy-rule romp of Canada in the World Baseball Classic–and also was from just three years ago.</p><p>“That was TA,” Hahn told the Sun-Times. “Teams were just better when he was in there and setting the tone, which is something he loved to do.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/mXT6EsnpnPU?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="A Letter to Chicago from Tim Anderson (2026)"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>He loved it, but as has been clear since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/10/tim-anderson-retirement-chicago-white-sox-southside-city-connect-uniforms-field-of-dreams-game" target="_blank" ><u>Anderson announced his retirement in an emotional Zoom session last month</u></a>, and even upon his return to Rate Field on Thursday night, it took a lot out of him.</p><p>“I looked at it like if I wasn't nervous, I wasn't ready,” Anderson said Thursday. “That first at-bat, I'm always nervous."</p><p>In Chicago early last season playing for the Angels, Anderson speculated that pushing himself to play through the nagging injuries late in his career also altered the mechanics of a swing that captured the 2019 batting title, and four-straight seasons of a .300 average or better. Others, including former teammates, felt his off-the-field mistakes wounded his once indomitable mindset.</p><p>Anderson felt it all, including the large platform his stardom brought, as an everpresent pressure that his enjoyment of the game stopped being able to out-pace. Just discussing his career prompted him to sweat profusely on his Zoom call in August, and before he addressed reporters in the Sox dugout on Thursday, he asked for a towel with which to dot his brow.</p><p>“I never wanted to be in that spotlight,” Anderson said. "I just wanted to be me, and that happened.”</p><p>Which remains a surreal sentiment for Anderson to express. Earlier this very decade, he felt built for the limelight, even more than he felt built to have a career longer than 991 major league games.</p><p>After Tarik Skubal was traded from the Tigers, Benetti found himself watching old video of Anderson ruining the two-time Cy Young winner’s major league debut; homering in the first at-bat of the game and lining an RBI double the following inning, amid a multi-year run of terrorizing Tiger pitching. Playoff games are what Anderson’s White Sox teams had too little of, especially since he had a career .485 postseason batting average.</p><p>“You could set anything up, and Tim Anderson was going to spike it out,” Benetti said. “He was going to make moments.</p><p>But only now is Anderson truly free to enjoy them. He covered his eyes and hugged his family as a scoreboard video segment of his career came to a close. Before that, he laughed about not having to worry about getting on time for a fastball Thursday night.</p><p>Back in the place where he was once at center stage, Anderson seemed content just to watch, and reflect.</p><p>“It's not what you did for me lately, it's what you did,” Anderson said. "Now, looking back at what I did: pretty cool. Pretty awesome, pretty dope, you know what I mean? It was a whole wave.”</p>

entries.title: Judgment day is coming for Sky coach Tyler Marsh
entries.summary: <p>After a disappointing year, some hard conversations are coming for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a>.</p><p>The big one will be with coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> about whether he’s earned a third season.</p><p>Marsh told the Sun-Times on Thursday he hasn’t yet discussed his job status with general manager <b>Jeff Pagliocca</b> or principal owner <b>Michael Alter</b>, and those conversations will be reserved for the offseason.</p><p>Until then, Marsh is full steam ahead.</p><p>“As long as I’m here I’m gonna give my best for this organization and these players and this city,” he said. "I can’t control what happens beyond that, but it’s never a question of if I want to be.”</p><p>“This is what I worked my whole life for. I haven’t had any handouts. I’ve worked and earned my way into an opportunity. You never know when these opportunities come the first time, or ever, and you don’t want to let them slip away.”</p><p>Should Marsh get the boot? On one hand, the Sky have a 30% win rate during Marsh’s tenure, the roster underperformed relative to its talent this year, and end-of-game management was an issue.</p><p>On the other hand, Marsh clearly improved this season, generally has strong relationships with players, and appears to have installed a viable offensive system.</p><p>But maybe the most important factor has nothing to do with Marsh. It’s whether Alter, Pagliocca and company think they can actually attract someone better. They do have an appealing young core in <b>Rickea Jackson</b>,<b> Sydney Taylor</b> and <b>Kamilla Cardoso</b> to go along with two first-round picks in 2027; maybe that’s enough to convince a top-tier coach to come on board.</p><p>But the organization still doesn’t have the best reputation. Nor do they have an All-Star on the roster or a chance at landing one in the lottery. It’s far from a perfect job.</p><p><b>Easy does it</b></p><p>When discussing how he'll manage rotations to close out the season, Marsh has repeatedly used phrases like "exercising caution,” “not wanting to overload anyone” and “preserving bodies.”</p><p>In other words: don’t expect the Sky to be at full throttle during their final week.</p><p><b>DiJonai Carrington</b> missed Thursday’s game against the Mystics managing her foot injury. <b>Natasha Cloud</b> has not been a full participant at practice and left after the first half (knee), and <b>Azurá Stevens</b> also told the Sun-Times that she and the health staff will be managing her knee.</p><p>The upside is that rookies <b>Gabriela Jaquez</b> and <b>Aicha Coulibaly</b> will get more playing time, which should be the priority at this point. But it also means any hope of Marsh strengthening his case with some upsets in the final week is probably naive.</p><p><b>Thank you, Chicago</b></p><p>Not only have the Mystics excelled ahead of schedule this season, they’re also on track to receive a 2027 lottery pick from the Sky.</p><p>That’s because of the pick swap included in the 2025 trade that brought Ariel Atkins to Chicago.</p><p>“Thank goodness [President of Monumental Basketball] Michael Winger and the folks back in D.C. have positioned us to have a lottery pick,” Mystics coach <b>Sydney Johnson</b> said before the game. “We’ll see what happens.”</p><p>As things stand, the Mystics are projected to receive the No. 3 pick, while the Sky would get No. 10 in return.</p><p>The Mystics also own the Sky's 2028 pick which they got in return for guard <b>Jacy Sheldon.</b></p>

entries.title: Francis W. Parker School's expansion gets first city approval, despite ire from neighbors
entries.summary: <p>The Francis W. Parker School scored a victory in its yearslong battle against some Lincoln Park neighbors over its plan to build a middle school on West Belden Avenue.</p><p>The school, which has been in Lincoln Park for 125 years, received approval Thursday for its expansion from the Chicago Plan Commission. The school also sought approval for new athletic field lights and security cameras. The project is now expected to go before the Committee on Zoning, Landmarks and Building Standards next week, according to the school.</p><p>Parker School said the additional building is needed because it has reached capacity at its current property, 330 W. Webster Ave. The private school teaches pre-K through 12th grade and has 940 students, according to a spokesperson. </p><p>It's proposing tearing down the 15-unit Belden by the Park condos at 335 W. Belden Ave. to build a five-story building, which would include a pedestrian overpass connecting the buildings. The new property would also have a multipurpose room and terraces, along with overflow classroom space. </p><p>Parker, which owns the condo building, pegs construction costs at $39 million.</p><p>The expansion would allow Parker to welcome 125 new students and add 30 permanent staff and faculty jobs to accommodate the growth, Principal Dan Frank told commissioners Thursday. The new students and faculty would gradually be added over the course of seven years.</p><p>“The building in our proposal is crucial to helping us achieve those goals because Parker is at capacity,” Frank said. “The only way to increase our student body and to add jobs is to expand our physical space.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-440000" name="image-440000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a3b305c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6487x3641+0+514/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F8f%2Fdd6d9dc9452fb77dbdbf12aa57d9%2Fplancom-260918-3-2.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2981fa5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6487x3641+0+514/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F8f%2Fdd6d9dc9452fb77dbdbf12aa57d9%2Fplancom-260918-3-2.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/85ee04e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6487x3641+0+514/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F8f%2Fdd6d9dc9452fb77dbdbf12aa57d9%2Fplancom-260918-3-2.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Francis W. Webster Ave. in Lincoln Park.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Parker said it’s been discussing the expansion with neighbors and nearby businesses since 2024, and the school has made concessions to address residents' concerns. </p><p>The pedestrian overpass, accessible on the new building’s third and fourth floors, was narrowed and moved farther east. The school is also relocating rooftop mechanical equipment to the east side of the roof, away from neighbors on the building's west side.</p><p>The building’s southwest corner was also cut back to create more natural light for neighboring townhomes, the development team said. And the nearby building at 317-25 W. Belden Ave., owned by Parker, will be kept as residential for the next 30 years, in response to neighborhood concerns over the loss of homes.</p><p>But neighbors still showed up in full force Thursday, with more than 40 people signed up to speak about the proposal. </p><p>Parents of Parker students, alumni and some board members spoke in favor of the proposal, citing the need to better position Parker for the future. But they were outnumbered by opponents of the project, many of whom were against the demolition of the 1909 vintage courtyard building at 335 W. Belden.</p><p>Preservation Chicago urged the commission to reject Parker’s proposal, citing the inclusion of Belden by the Park in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/06/26/chicago-stock-courtyard-buildings-wind-up-national-register-historic-places" >courtyard building landmark district</a> the group has pursued for a number of years.</p><p>Some detractors pointed to the <a class="Link" href="https://eastlincolnparkneighbors.net/a-better-proposal" target="_blank" >Better Plan</a>, a proposal created by the group East Lincoln Park Neighbors that calls for a five-story building on Parker’s parking lot and a sixth-story aquatic center, to avoid demolishing residential buildings.</p><p>Michelle Hoppe Villegas, board member of the Mid-North Association, said its board opposes the expansion.</p><p>“We ask that you listen to the overwhelming public opposition to amending the current plan development agreement and ask that you reject the private institution … asking to encroach upon our dense and treasured historic neighborhood,” Hoppe Villegas said. “If allowed, Parker will consume and gut this historic community.”</p><p>East Lincoln Park Neighbors said in a statement that Thursday's "vote reflects a rushed and inadequate review of a proposal with lasting consequences for the neighborhood. Chicago’s planning process should welcome genuine community engagement, require timely disclosure of key information, and ensure that public bodies fully scrutinize major developments before approving them. Today, it fell short on all counts.”</p><p>Anny Gary, member of Parker’s board of trustees, said the school’s proposal is the result of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2020/5/21/21266563/lincoln-park-condo-owners-francis-parker-school-lawsuit-straw-buyers" >years of dialogue</a>. She said the Better Plan isn’t viable and overestimates the amount of developable land in the parking lot by about 35% to 40%.</p><p>“This Proposal is the product of years of collaboration — with neighbors, community groups, local elected officials, and the Parker community — all working together to shape a plan that benefits not only Parker students, but our community and the city of Chicago as a whole,” a Parker spokesperson said in a statement. “From expanding access and financial assistance for Chicago students to bringing new affordable housing and enhanced safety measures to Lincoln Park, this plan reflects Parker's 125-year commitment to being a responsible, engaged neighbor and civic partner."</p><p>The school expects construction to start no sooner than 2028.</p><p>Separately, the Plan Commission approved the proposal for a 19-unit, mixed-income apartment building at 665 W. Sheridan Road and a Fulton Market high-rise, with more than 400 units.</p><p>Northwestern Memorial Hospital’s proposed hospital tower at 330 E. Erie St. also received its first city approval. The 1.2 million-square-foot tower will create more than 200 new patient beds and employ more than 1,000 workers when complete. It’s estimated to cost $1.5 billion and would be completed in 2031, if approved by the City Council.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2020/5/21/21266563/lincoln-park-condo-owners-francis-parker-school-lawsuit-straw-buyers" >Condo owners allege Francis W. Parker School tried to fraudulently take over their building, call the move ‘morally bankrupt’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Man, 29, shot while sitting in car in Morgan Park
entries.summary: <p>A man was hospitalized Thursday after he was shot in the neck while inside a vehicle in Morgan Park, police said. </p><p>Police said the victim, a 29-year-old man, sustained a single gunshot wound to the neck at about 8 p.m. when someone fired at the vehicle in the 1100 block of West 114th Place. </p><p>The man was reportedly a passenger in the vehicle when the gunman appeared from a nearby alley and fired shots, police said.</p><p>He was transported to Christ Hospital and is listed in good condition, police said. </p><p>Area 2 detectives are investigating the shooting.</p>

entries.title: 2 women wounded after being shot in Chatham alley
entries.summary: <p>A 56-year-old woman was wounded after being shot in an alley in Chatham late Thursday, police said.</p><p>At about 8:12 p.m., police said the woman was walking in an alley in the 8100 block of South Maryland Avenue when she reportedly heard a verbal altercation and saw a 23-year-old woman run to the area from a nearby apartment complex, being pursued by a man. The man then pulled a gun and fired several shots at the woman. </p><p>One of the rounds hit the 56-year-old woman in the leg. The 23-year-old woman sustained a graze wound to her legs, police said.</p><p>The injured 56-year-old woman was treated at the scene before being transported to the University of Chicago Medical Center in good condition. The other woman refused treatment and was listed in good condition.</p><p>Area 2 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Illinois Restaurant Association chief calls out uneven enforcement of sidewalk cafe lights rule
entries.summary: <p>The head of the Illinois Restaurant Association says Chicago's uneven enforcement of rules banning strings of sparkling lights for outdoor dining areas is unfair to restaurant owners, who are already struggling.</p><p>President Sam Toia made the comments following the city's crackdown against one <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/12/lights-roscoe-village-cafes-bacp-outdoor-dining" >Roscoe Village restaurant’s outdoor lights</a> — even as scores of other restaurants hang them over sidewalks and parkways.</p><p>Lush Wine & Spirits, 2232 W. Roscoe St., was ordered in March to remove its decorative white lights after an inspector from the city's Department of Business Affairs and Consumer Protection said they got a complaint about Lush's lights.</p><p>Until then, Lush owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/02/07/lush-wine-spirits-roscoe-village-einhorn-tariffs" >Mitch Einhorn</a> — who has a sidewalk cafe permit — says he'd never heard of any law against hanging lights. Other eateries along Roscoe Street still use similar lights, as do dozens, if not hundreds, of other businesses citywide.</p><p>Toia says the BACP's complaint-driven system has created an uneven playing field for Chicago restaurants and it needs to stop.</p><p>"If there is a reason why they're telling us this is a hazard, then explain it because most restaurateurs are restaurateurs. They're not electricians. They're not building inspectors," Toia says. "They need to go deeper and tell us why. They need to tell us what the issue is and how to do it right. Otherwise, they need to let it go."</p><p>This summer, the Chicago Sun-Times spotted at least 40 eateries with outdoor lights on about 12 blocks along Lincoln Avenue and West Fulton Market and Randolph streets.</p><p>The strings of lights are typically draped high above the sidewalk. Some are attached to nearby parkway trees or city light poles; others are hung on wooden pergolas covering eating areas.</p><p>Many are plugged into outdoor outlets or hooked up to extension cords that are flush against the sides of buildings. In some cases, cords are hidden inside a conduit mounted on a pergola.</p><p>Spokespersons for the Chicago Department of Buildings and the Department of Transportation say the law banning lights is <a class="Link" href="https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/chicago/latest/chicago_il/0-0-0-2652655" target="_blank" ><u>Chapter 10-29</u></a> of the Municipal Code of Chicago, which governs "wires, pipes, cables and conduits on, under or over public property" — with public property, in this case, being city sidewalks and parkways.</p><p>But the law seems to allow for some wiggle room.</p><p>The ordinance says wires or cables aren't allowed "without first having obtained a permit issued by the department of transportation after consultation with the office of emergency management and communications."</p><p>Einhorn says he asked BACP how to apply for a permit to make his lights legal and was told there is no application process.</p><p>Staff at Ald. Matt Martin's (47th) office emailed the Sun-Times saying they're "aware of this issue and are working with BACP to identify a path forward for sidewalk cafes to have string lights, whether that is a procedure change or a legislative one."</p><p>Ald. Debra Silverstein (50th), who chairs the City Council committee overseeing BACP, says “small businesses are already facing enormous challenges, and the city should be looking for ways to support them, not finding new ways to fine them."</p><p>"I intend to review this issue with my colleagues and explore whether there are legislative options to provide greater clarity and protect small business owners while maintaining appropriate safety standards," Silverstein says.</p><p>Elisa Sledzinska, BACP’s deputy commissioner for communications and outreach, says in an email that the department, which administers the city's sidewalk cafe program, is simply enforcing the municipal code.</p><p>"BACP uses CDOT and DOB [Department of Buildings] guidance to issue permits. BACP does not have an opinion on this law; we enforce the Municipal Code of Chicago. CDOT has shared that lights in and of themselves would not be a violation, but if they are stringing/hanging cables, wires or conduits on City assets or across the right of way that would be a violation," Sledzinska says.</p><p>Lights are a fixture of outdoor cafes in metropolitan areas around the country.</p><p>Toia says at a time when restaurants are fighting for survival amid rising food, labor and operating costs, every little bit helps — including strings of white lights that create a romantic and enticing atmosphere for outdoor diners.</p><p>"It's ambience. It brings a healing. It brings a European feeling — eating outside with some lights. It's kind of the aesthetics," he says.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/12/lights-roscoe-village-cafes-bacp-outdoor-dining" >Lights out for a Roscoe Village cafe’s outdoor dining — even as others shine on</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Every fear about Bears' defense materialized in season opener, leaving DC Dennis Allen to problem solve
entries.summary: <p>After <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> allowed 37 points and 478 yards to the Panthers, defensive coordinator Dennis Allen’s response to the first question at his weekly news conference Thursday began with, “I’m not going to spend a lot of time talking about last week.”</p><p>Don’t you think we should? There’s plenty to discuss.</p><p>It’s rare for a team to score that many points and get blown out, as the Panthers did <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/13/bears-inactives-vs-panthers-for-week-1-backup-qb-tyson-bagent-inactive-but-designated-as-emergency-3rd-qb" >in their 59-37 loss to the Bears</a>. Over the previous five seasons, teams that scored at least 37 went 223-18-2, and all the losses were by six or fewer points.</p><p>This might be tough to accept, but the Bears won’t put up 59 every week. It’ll be a battle just to get to 30 against the Vikings and defensive coordinator Brian Flores on Sunday.</p><p>The Panthers have an unproven quarterback in Bryce Young and were 27th in total offense last season. But almost every NFL quarterback, even backups, can play effectively if given time in the pocket. Between that luxury and the Bears’ lapses in the secondary, Young played one of the best games of his career with 361 yards, three touchdown passes and a 110.3 passer rating.</p><p>The performance was a portrait of every pessimistic hypothetical about this defense materializing — and then some.</p><p>Last season, the Bears were unsteady defensively. They often rescued themselves by forcing a league-high 33 turnovers, but weren’t good at two essentials for any good defense: stopping the run and pressuring the quarterback.</p><p>They demonstrated an exaggerated version of that formula against the Panthers. The Bears allowed 5.7 yards per rush and sacked Young twice. Their three takeaways, including one on special teams, might’ve been the only thing that kept the Panthers from scoring in the 50s themselves and taking the game down to the end.</p><p>On top of that, one of the few pieces the Bears believed they could count on was cornerback Jaylon Johnson, and he and Tyrique Stevenson both struggled.</p><p>All this talk about last week must be killing Allen.</p><p>But it’s relevant because of what comes next.</p><p>Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell is one of the sharpest offensive minds in the game and has somehow posted a .638 winning percentage despite a carousel of quarterbacks. His team embarrassed the Packers last week with touchdowns on four consecutive drives to close the game and win 39-22.</p><p>That was with castoff Carson Wentz at quarterback since castoff Kyler Murray exited early with a concussion and soon-to-be castoff J.J. McCarthy is buried on the bench. O’Connell is just that good. Whoever starts out of Wentz and Murray is a threat to exceed what Young did.</p><p>The Vikings have a top-10 offensive line, an elite wide receiver in Justin Jefferson, an excellent No. 2 receiver in Jordan Addison, two-time Pro Bowl tight end T.J. Hockenson and four-time 1,000-yard rusher Aaron Jones.</p><p>Sweating yet?</p><p>“Week 1 is no indication of Week 2,” Allen said.</p><p>Sure, but here’s the issue: What’s going to change?</p><p>Johnson should play better, but otherwise, the answers aren’t obvious. Other than waiting on nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon to be activated next month, there’s no help on the way. That leaves it to Allen to problem solve the way coach Ben Johnson does on offense.</p><p>Because hoping for 59 points each week isn’t a plan.</p>

entries.title: Destroying Head Start limits our country's future
entries.summary: <p>Like nearly 40 million other Americans, I'm a Head Start alumna. For my parents, childcare was an expensive proposition, so while my veteran father enrolled in community college, he enrolled me in childcare. It was my earliest community, a place where first friendships were formed, self-awareness was cultivated and curiosity was exponential.</p><p>For over 60 years, Head Start has been the great equalizer, a pathway out of poverty that understands a child's early education, health and economic opportunity set the stage for an abundant future. Today, the Department of Health and Human Services wants to dismantle what makes it so effective.</p><p>The proposed changes include removing staff-to-child ratio mandates, overcrowding classrooms and overwhelming teachers. HHS also wants to do away with evidence-based math and literacy standards, risking children's kindergarten readiness. It would also cut support for infants, children with disabilities, and dual-language learners.</p><p>HHS says these changes will cut red tape and free up money for the program. But efficiency doesn't mean gutting the national benchmarks that guarantee quality. The department also frames this as giving states and parents more control. However, this proposal weakens parents' voices in their children's learning and development, and it disempowers credentialed childcare operators.</p><p>Quality early education is prohibitively expensive for many families. Those who can afford it pay for private preschools with small classes, credentialed teachers and rigorous curricula. Head Start was built on the premise that those standards shouldn't be reserved for whoever can pay for them.</p><p>Fortunately, these proposed changes aren’t final. I’m calling on everyone impacted by Head Start to speak out about what makes this program so special. The proposal is <a class="Link" href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/07/2026-16134/reducing-federal-burden-for-head-start-programs" target="_blank" >open to public comment </a>in the Federal Register until Oct. 6.</p><p><i>Nicole Robinson, CEO of YWCA Metropolitan Chicago</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7a0000" name="module-7a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Teens need accessible third spaces</h3><p>The story <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/moment-of-youth/2026/09/10/teen-beach-gathering-conflict" >“ ‘Zero fights’ at a Chicago teen beach gathering, but some adults left youth feeling discouraged”</a> demonstrates how extraordinarily difficult it is for teens to find spaces where they can gather and enjoy themselves.</p><p>When I was a teenager, I never had to secure a municipal permit, establish a security checkpoint, coordinate funding and transportation, or recruit chaperones to enjoy what my community had to offer. Organizing a two-person picnic would've been a stretch for me back then. Thankfully, the young people who worked with the city and Project Exploration to help plan a permitted, supervised teen beach party are brighter, more organized, and more committed than I ever was at their ages.</p><p>Despite all their planning, however, their event encountered some difficulty with adult volleyball players who wanted to use the nets in the area the teens had reserved.</p><p>We don't want teens taking over Downtown, but we don't provide the spaces they need to be themselves. We want teens to invest their energy in productive outlets, but then we tear down the positive things they build. We're expecting solutions from the people whose solutions we keep rejecting.</p><p>If we want to solve the "teen takeover" issue, we need to make it simpler for third spaces catering to young people to open and thrive.</p><p>In Chicago, whether you want to run the Salt Shed or just want to host a poetry reading in a tiny cafe, you need the same kind of license.</p><p>Any community business that wants to welcome young people into their space with fun activities or entertainment will have to first tackle zoning variations, byzantine applications and pay tens of thousands of dollars in fees.</p><p>What if, instead of ineffective snap curfews (that are rendered unenforceable with a big enough group), we had a movement of community-focused young people in coalition with small businesses to create the third spaces young people need to help our city thrive into the future? Let’s change city laws and public attitudes to make that vision possible.</p><p><i>Noah Bazis, University of Chicago Law School</i></p><p></p><h3>Save this historic church</h3><p>Don't lose what you already have going for the community, because once it’s gone, it's gone, metaphorically speaking.</p><p>I respectfully disagree with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/09/05/city-methodist-church-largest-midwest-gary-demolition" >Lauren Pacheco’s statement</a> that it's not always possible for every historical site to be saved. It can be done, and has been done across the country. This is true of and for all structures. It just takes foresight and effort in many capacities.</p><p>I happened to see the recent headline while perusing social media, and it made me think, "What a beautiful and magnificent structure, even in ruin form."</p><p>The church has so much potential for a communal space. Perhaps an arts and cultural museum, entertainment venue, an arboretum, additional housing, lodging, etc. The city could harness investments like grants from the state’s historical society, state bonding bill, and/or maybe partner with the very company that helped develop the aforementioned.</p><p>I do hope that Gary assesses its historical value and works with what you already have established. New isn’t always better. Redevelopment doesn’t always bring a fresh start in ways intended to take full advantage of a creative concept turned into reality.</p><p>The structure is an artist’s blank canvas to create. It's worth fighting for.</p><p><i>Rhett Abrahamson, Duluth, Minnesota</i></p>

entries.title: Mark 'DJ Ice Box' Josephson, an early champion of Chicago rap, has died at 58
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p>The only hint that Highland Park attorney Mark Josephson played a significant role in the history of Chicago's rap scene is the password he chose for his home Wi-Fi network — a lyric from a Public Enemy song.</p><p>In 1986, he was a University of Chicago student majoring in Near Eastern languages and and civilizations when he started spinning records at the university's radio station WHPK-FM 88.5 under the name DJ Ice Box.</p><p>He was one in a trio of volunteer student DJs — all of them white — who rotated at the helm of a late-night rap show that first went on the air in 1984, playing rap on the air in Chicago at a time mainstream radio stations wouldn't touch the emerging genre.</p><p>Mr. Josephson died July 19. He suffered from frontotemporal dementia and ALS. He was 58.</p><p>WHPK's low-powered, 100-watt signal reached most of the South Side and became a lifeline for many young Black people who had limited access to the music, which wasn't widely available in record stores at the time.</p><p>"We stumbled across WHPK one day in the mid-'80s when we turned the radio dial all the way to the left and heard some static-y rapping, and we were like, 'Man! They rapping," said Darrell "Artistic" Roberts, one of a group of teenage rappers who grew up near 101st and State streets who called themselves the Curfew Crew. </p><p>They rap-battled teenagers from other neighborhoods and would tape the show so they could listen to the music again and again.</p><p>Mr. Josephson and his fellow DJs didn't just play rap they gleaned from record stores in New York City, where rap originated. They also played rap tapes that Chicago rappers dropped off at the college radio station. That local talent would call in from a payphone outside the station, and the DJs would come down to pick up their tapes. Sometimes, they'd invite the young rappers to hang out at the station.</p><p>That's how Roberts got his first rap song on the air.</p><p>Roberts and C. "Kingdom Rock" Sanders, a rapper who says he was one of WHPK's first interns, are founders of the Chicago Hip Hop Heritage Museum.</p><p>Of Mr. Josephson, Sanders said: "He was a slender, Caucasian, Jewish man with glasses and an Afro, and you would not expect him to be playing the music he was playing. He was unassumingly hip-hop."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-250000" class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>John Schauer, who spun records alongside Mr. Josephson as J.P. Chill, said that, as white DJs, they never tried to be anything they weren't.</p><p>"Mark and I were not like the sort of Black African American vernacular English adopting people," he said. "We were just like, 'We are who we are.' We were different, and we were accepted."</p><p>It was obvious the DJs were white guys playing music created by Black people, but skin color didn't pose a barrier, Sanders said.</p><p>"They were white, we were Black, but our spirits connected us to the culture, and to this day we always pay homage to WHPK DJs," Roberts said.</p><p>"Most people think of Kanye, Common, Twista when they think of Chicago rappers because they reached another plateau of success, but there's a lot of local artists who paved the way for those guys who were played on WHPK, which really broke ground for hip-hop culture being nurtured here in Chicago before all these other stations got on board," Sanders said.</p><p>"It's hard to fathom in this day and age, where all of recorded music is available to everyone at all times, but <b>Black</b> people couldn't hear the music anywhere else," Schauer said.</p><p>Mr. Josephson DJed during his time as a U. of C. student and for eight years after graduating. After law school at Northwestern University, he worked for the Department of Justice's tax division and for then-Attorney General Lisa Madigan. </p><p>He moved from Hyde Park to Highland Park, where he and his wife raised their family.</p><p>In 2024, Mr. Josephson had a full-circle moment. He was attending a Common show at Millennium Park for the park's 20th anniversary celebration. It turned out he'd been among the first DJs to play Common's music on the air. And he was wearing a WHPK T-shirt. He ended up chatting with others at the show, who used to listen to his college broadcasts.</p><p>"Even though I knew my dad's history, it was surreal to see a bunch of middle-aged Black guys get so excited to meet my dad," said his son, Ari Josephson. "It was the first public evidence I had of the impact he had."</p><p>Mr. Josephson would go hear other types of live music, too, often indie rock, and made a hobby of taping the performances, most of the time with the artist's permission.</p><p>One of his favorites was a 1989 George Clinton show that he likened to a "religious experience."</p><p>His girlfriend and future wife Lea Josephson was there, too. She remembers thinking, "What is this? Oh, this is phenomenal!"</p><p>Mr. Josephson's concert companion for years was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/05/04/aadam-jacobs-online-archive-tapes-concerts" >Aadam Jacobs, </a>whose collection of thousands of taped concerts is being <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2026/05/04/aadam-jacobs-online-archive-tapes-concerts" target="_blank" >digitized and uploaded onto the Internet Archive</a>, where they will be available for free to anyone who wants to listen.</p><p>Jacobs said he expects that some concerts Mr. Josephson taped also will be available on the archive.</p><p>"It was just a real love for doing what made us happy that we shared, and I'm so glad I found someone like him to be able to go on adventures with," Jacobs said. "I'm really sad he's gone. He was a great buddy."</p><p>Mr. Josephson was born in Skokie on Aug. 24, 1967, to Helene and Eliott Josephson. She was an office worker. He was an accountant. He grew up in Northbrook and attended Glenbrook North High School.</p><p>He was a jeans and T-shirt kind of guy. Now, his family is figuring out what to do with his massive collection of concert T-shirts.</p><p>He incorporated his Ice Box moniker into his personal email and social media handle and occasionally used his DJ background in the icebreaker game Two Truths and a Lie.</p><p>In addition to his wife and son, Mr. Josephson is survived by a daughter, Shayna Josephson. Services have been held.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Friend Grows Distant After Personal Struggle
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> A dear friend of 10 years experienced a severe mental health crisis. I did my best to reach out to her, but she pushed me away and flaked on plans and important events at the last minute at least a dozen times. Once her mental health began to improve, I approached her and told her I understood her behavior had been largely out of her control, but it still hurt when she pushed me away and canceled at the last minute for meaningful events in my life. She apologized, I accepted, and I thought we could move on again as close friends.</p><p>She is now engaged to a man and seems to put no time or value into our friendship. I am grieving the loss of a dear friend and struggling to accept that it is over. I have many questions: Did we simply drift apart? Is her new fiance more important to her? Is she upset that I confronted her, and was I wrong to do so? Do 10 years of friendship mean nothing? I'm afraid another difficult conversation will create a worse outcome, but I miss the friend I once had. Where is the line to excuse behavior under the duress of mental health and at what point do I simply accept that she is no longer a good friend, mental health crisis aside? — <i>NOT OVER IT IN OREGON</i></p><p><b>DEAR NOT OVER IT:</b> As much as this close friendship may have meant to you, it's time to realize that these relationships are not always static. They can evolve, devolve and change. You were within your rights to express to the woman that you felt pushed away during her mental health crisis. Those were your feelings, and you were entitled to them.</p><p>The time has come now for you to lighten up. Your friend is happily engaged to someone who makes her happy, and her attention and priorities have shifted away from her close friendship with you. Of course her fiance is more important to her than you are. It isn't that you are no longer good friends, it's that the intensity has lessened. Handle that as you wish, but I see nothing positive to be gained by another confrontation.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My daughter is getting married to "Bob," who has an 8-year-old son, "Ricky," from a previous marriage. The plan was to have Bob's son be the ring bearer and have my 2½-year-old grandson, "Aiden," be the flower boy. However, Ricky has autism, and Bob has decided that it would be better to not include him in the ceremony. Now he says he doesn't want Aiden to be in the ceremony, either. I can understand Bob's feelings, but it does not seem fair to me. — <i>NEW MEXICO GRANDDAD</i></p><p><b>DEAR GRANDDAD:</b> You may feel let down by this decision, but trust that your grandson will never know the difference. When planning a wedding, the bride and groom organize the ceremony in whatever way they feel will best celebrate their union. Fairness doesn't play a role in it, and no one is owed a place in the wedding party. Attend the wedding with joy in your heart, and show your daughter how much you love her by respecting her decision.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In “The Attic: Things I’ve Seen While Lying on My Back,” Chicago actress Tyler Meredith plays Shana Carroll, whose battle with metastatic breast cancer is captured in acrobatics. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Milissa Martin</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>So instead of one-of-a-kind, oddball experiences, we watch Tyler Meredith (the veteran Chicago actress playing Carroll) narrate from beneath the beams of her childhood attic, the place of the show’s title. We see her marvel at dust motes glittering in the air, the awkwardness of a middle-school dance. We see her giving birth, even considering her own death. </p><p>And her experiences are amplified through nine acrobats’ extraordinary feats of grace, physical strength and dexterity: three-story human towers on the move, bodies flung in the air and (seemingly) effortlessly caught. And in one sequence that made the audience gasp, acrobat Melvin Diggs plummets head first down the 20-foot length of a steel pole, stopping inches from the stage floor.</p><p>One of the show’s most innovative and memorable scenes is toward the end, when Carroll’s character is lying in a hospital bed that gently rises from the horizontal to the vertical. Hands poke through the mattress from below, grabbing at Meredith’s writhing body. It’s less B-movie horror than a clever way to illustrate her ambivalence toward hospitals.</p><p>“When you’re alone in a hospital bed, it both feels like they won’t stop fussing with me — and the creepiness of it — but it also feels like you have accompaniment and comfort even though you’re so alone,” Carroll said.</p><p>In the show, the bed then swings, trapeze-like, high above the stage with Meredith lying still on it.</p><p>Though Carroll now directs others to fly through the air, she says she is able to use the lessons of a life on the trapeze in her cancer battle.</p><p>“There is a lot of pain. You burn your skin. You get bruises everywhere,” Carroll said.</p><p>And there are similarities between the fear she faced during every performance and the fear of confronting her mortality.</p><p>“With cancer, you don’t choose it, but it feels familiar: ‘Oh, I’ve been here, I know how to navigate fear,’” she said. “You feel like you’ve confronted death before.”</p>

entries.title: In “Liliom,” making its Chicago premiere at the Joffrey, the soundtrack is as ambitious as the steps
entries.summary: <p>Earlier this week at the Lyric Opera House, the stage was set for the Joffrey Ballet’s “Liliom,” a story ballet receiving its American-company premiere. A small carousel sat, unrevolving, to the audience’s right, and a lonely bench at the left. Upstage from the center-stage dance floor and perched above where the action would unfold, a platform housed a big band of 15 musicians.</p><p>“This is where the dancers start looking for downbeats,” said Nathan Brock, the conductor. He was addressing not just the big band, but also a more standard 50-plus-member orchestra, nestled in its customary place in the pit. Brock was situated a long way from the band, and they were about to wrestle with the disparity in the speed of light and the speed of sound.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" And it’s stylistically eclectic, the jazz weaving its way in and out of the classical-tradition music, which itself careers around from lush stringy sounds to circusy waltzes to accordion-led French street music. entries.title: EDM sister duo Krewella hits another peak with first new album in 4 years
entries.summary: <p>Without the Northbrook Public Library, Krewella may have never happened.</p><p>“It was an embassy of music for us and an incredible resource for records. We’d dive into the treasure chest of CDs and then rent them and upload them at home on iTunes,” recalls Jahan Yousaf. Along with younger sister Yasmine, the duo first plotted out the electronic dance music project in 2007 while still enrolled at Glenbrook North High School, armed with their library finds like the Cranberries and the Doors and their parents’ music collection of ABBA, Bollywood and Arabic music. “Another huge influence for us was pirating music with Napster or LimeWire,” Jahan added, laughing at the antiquated memories.</p><p>Old-school technology is a major theme on Krewella’s latest album “Peak,” which abounds with messages about our collective obsession with the proverbial hottest new things and trying to find euphoria in an ever-changing world. The artwork plays this up too, showing the sisters lounging around on stacks of old laptops, printers, fax machines and monitors, all captured at an e-waste recycling center in Los Angeles where the two now live.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-160000" name="module-160000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Krewella</h3><br><b>When:</b> 10 p.m., Sept. 19<br><b>Where:</b> Sound-Bar, 226 W. Ontario St.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $28<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://sound-bar.com/" target="_blank" >sound-bar.com</a></div> </div><p>“Everything you see are props made out of people's old things,” said Yasmine. “Each single one of them held someone's entire life on them – all their conversations, all their work, and then suddenly it's obsolete and gone and thrown away. We felt it was really important to capture the feeling of how temporary everything is … while trying to be present with how fast things are moving,” she added. “We hope this album helps people maybe sort through some of the impending changes of our world and who we want to be during them.”</p><p>Grappling with the life twists and thinking about “how things used to be” takes on extra meaning for the sisters (now 34 and 37) as they return home to play Sound-Bar Sept. 19, after hopefully catching some Riot Fest sets. “Jahan loves Tool and I love Morrissey,” Yasmine said. (Krewella’s set takes place after the festival in Douglass Park wraps for the day, for anyone who wants to pull a similar doubleheader.)</p><p>Coming home makes Jahan “remember a lot of funny club scene Chicago stuff,” she said, thinking back fondly to Krewella’s first show at Cobra Lounge during the venue’s former Zombies vs. Skeletons punk-hardcore-EDM crossover series on Wednesday nights. Or how they used to live across from the once-reigning nightclub The Mid in Fulton Market. Or how one of the first times they were at Sound-Bar was when they snuck in an underage Yasmine to film parts of their 2012 video “Killin’ It.” It appears on the 2012 “Play Hard” EP alongside the emotive Top 40 hit “Alive” that put Krewella on the map.</p><p>Back then, it was a halcyon time for the sisters (and former bandmate/producer Kristopher Trindl), who found themselves signed to Columbia Records, earning Hot 100 hits on the Billboard<i> </i>charts and dominating the festival circuit at Electric Daisy Carnival, Ultra Music Festival and hometown events such as Perry’s Stage at Lollapalooza and Spring Awakening, at a time when women didn’t have the same presence in EDM circles as they do now.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" The label name is a nod to their Pakistani and German-Lithuanian background.</p></figcaption></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>That “peak” of Krewella’s career hit Yasmine when the new album was released Sept. 4 on the duo’s Mixed Kids Records, which they founded in 2017 after mutually parting ways with Columbia Records. The label name is a nod to their Pakistani and German-Lithuanian background. “I had this huge wave of tears come over me because I was so present with the feeling of being one of the very few women who has been allowed to walk through the door. I was like, ‘wow, my sister and I have made a place here,’” Yasmine said. “And I feel so grateful for the place that we have.”</p><p>“Peak” comes after a four-year break for Krewella, including two years during which they didn’t touch music at all. Jahan took up cooking and working with Nagar Women’s Health House, a nonprofit clinic in Northern Pakistan that she co-founded with family and community members during the pandemic. “When we first started, we would hear stories about women dying on the side of the road during childbirth. … The universe has given us so much to be well resourced, to take care of ourselves. So that's our way of giving back in Pakistan,” she said.</p><p>And Yasmine “side quested really hard” on a project she wants to remain mum about in case she wants to return to it someday. But both recognize the break was a necessary one. “I don't think we could have done it right after our last record [2022’s “The Body Never Lies”] because I was pretty burnt out. The thought of making music again felt impossible, and if I had done it, it would have been forced. People would have heard it. And I don't want to fill the space with music that wasn't made from the heart,” Yasmine said. </p><p>But there’s something about coming back to the scene in 2026 that feels serendipitous, at a time when Chicago DJs, producers and electronic artists are having a moment. Artists like Honey Dijon, who’s finding continued global status; a resurgent Green Velvet, who played both Beyond Wonderland and ARC this year; and, of course, John Summit, whose banner year included a groundbreaking headlining set at Lollapalooza and a return to United Center for a two-night stand in November. Though for the Krewella sisters, that’s how they’ve always seen Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: In Gary, Indiana, a month after historic NIPSCO power outage, families still wait for relief
entries.summary: <p>Inside Melissa Dixon’s home in Gary, the lights are back on. Her refrigerator is working. And she’s playing music as she does yard work. The generator that she had on her front steps is gone now. </p><p>It's more than a month since Dixon and hundreds of thousands of others in Gary and across northwest Indiana were left without power, some for at least <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/graphics/weather/powerless/12-nights-without-power-in-Gary-Indiana/" target="_blank" ><u>two weeks</u></a>, and she's still feeling anxious.</p><p>It wasn’t until recently that she finally did a big grocery haul. Until then, she'd been buying only enough food for a day or two.</p><p>“I don’t want to put food in here or buy food for a couple days,” Dixon says, “because I don’t want to lose my food again.”</p><p>She was among nearly 375,000 of the Northern Indiana Public Service Company's customers — of the 500,000 it serves — who were without electricity for days after an Aug. 11 derecho. </p><p>Gusts of 99 miles an hour were recorded at the Gary/Chicago International Airport. But Gary was one of the last communities to have power fully restored, U.S. Rep. Frank Mrvan, D-Indiana, whose congressional district includes Gary, said in a letter to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission asking for a federal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/08/31/indianas-governor-demands-probe-of-power-utility-during-tour-of-storm-ravaged-gary" target="_blank" ><u>investigation</u></a> of NIPSCO’s The church organized food giveaways and opened to neighbors who were without power. Now, the Rev. Eric Boone, Tree of Life's senior pastor, says families in Gary are staying afloat, but things aren’t completely back to normal. Some people regained power only to find out their refrigerators no longer worked, he says.</p><p>“Even though lights came on, people’s bank accounts didn’t bounce back,” Boone says. “People’s food, refrigerators and freezers didn’t bounce back. Some people got mold. Some people’s houses are wrecked. Some people lost their cars.”</p><h3>Health worries</h3><p>Outside Dixon’s home, a large tree branch that had fallen on a neighbor’s property has been cut into smaller pieces. That's for firewood she plans to keep in case another storm knocks out the power again.</p><p>Inside, Dixon has stocked her refrigerator with staples like milk and eggs. She gets waffles to satisfy her four daughters, who range in age from 12 to 22 years old. Her younger daughters are all back in school. The house is mostly quiet with them in class. But steps from the kitchen, Dixon says she's worried about dark spots along the walls in her basement. Maybe those are mold. She keeps two humidifiers running in the basement, where she typically sleeps.</p><p>“We’re sick because of the mold,” Dixon says. “I started feeling really weird, like my vision … a lot of pain in my face and my neck area and going down my arm and my shoulder.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" She was taking medicine to try to treat inflammation that has led to facial nerve problems.</p><p>She'd like to move her family out of her home temporarily — until she’s able to get it checked for mold and any necessary remediation. </p><p>But first she needs some support. She applied for disaster relief through the Federal Emergency Management Agency, but her application is still pending.</p><p>The only financial help she has gotten is a $150 voucher from her township. Calling hotline after hotline has been like trying to win a contest rather than just get relief after a natural disaster.</p><p>“It’s like calling a radio station,” she says. “‘Ooh, am I going to win these tickets?’”</p><h3></h3><p>Dixon is among more than 33,000 people in Lake County, Indiana, who have applied for relief money from FEMA. The federal agency says $48.19 million has been allocated for Lake County but didn't say how many applications have been approved.</p><p>Gary officials distributed an additional $500,000 in disaster relief to about 1,200 households. In a city of about 67,000 people, that’s also only a fraction of the possible need.</p><p>Shanequa Cauley is among those in Gary who have struck out on getting help. She lost power for about nine days. It took much longer for her employer's power to be restored. That meant she lost out on about three weeks of pay.</p><p>Cauley says she borrowed from a friend to pay her rent on time. Some of the meals she and her 7-year-old daughter ate during the first weeks after the storm came from the City Life Center, which provided free hot meals to families in Gary. The center later gave out vouchers for $300 to use at a grocery store.</p><p>But those meals have since ended. Cauley is hopeful she can get her finances in better shape before the end of the month.</p><p>“I’m praying by next week everything should be good,” says Cauley, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/25/nipsco-filed-application-for-customer-rate-increases-amid-storm-that-ravaged-northwest-indiana" target="_blank" ><u>owes NIPSCO</u></a> about $89. “The first thing I’m going to do is get my NIPSCO caught up.”</p><h3>‘Refuse to be knocked out’</h3><p>Britney Rice, community adaptation program manager for the American Red Cross in Indiana, says caseworkers have been trying to connect Gary residents with the resources they need. Twenty-eight people are still living in temporary shelter, according to Rice, who says the Red Cross also assisted others in getting vouchers to stay at a hotel for 30 days.</p><p>Some people haven’t been able to replace the food they lost during the outage. For others, the Red Cross is helping get them into a better situation than they were before the storms, which could include helping them find a better job, Rice says.</p><p>“When people have been impacted by disasters and the trauma that goes along with it, and they kind of kick into survival mode, sometimes all they can see is what’s in front of them,” Rice says. “And they make decisions that, if they could have seen something much bigger, then they would have made bigger decisions.”</p><p>Boone says his Tree of Life congregation has been scrambling to get relief information out. There still are people trying to figure out how to get by, he says. But Boone says he’s been heartened by how people in Gary have come together.</p><p>“We are strong," Boone says. "We are some that don’t give in or give up easily. We might get knocked down, but we refuse to be knocked out.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d40000" name="image-d40000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3ebe81d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6313x3543+0+334/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff0%2F4a%2Fc73f88564d73b521ba913da2056d%2Fgaryupdate-260920-07.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c138c50/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6313x3543+0+334/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff0%2F4a%2Fc73f88564d73b521ba913da2056d%2Fgaryupdate-260920-07.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9473b45/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6313x3543+0+334/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff0%2F4a%2Fc73f88564d73b521ba913da2056d%2Fgaryupdate-260920-07.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Melissa Dixon still got a NIPSCO bill for $374. entries.title: Why Trump's tariffs are illegal
entries.summary: <p>President Donald Trump is trying to "shift the exercise of core tariff authority from Congress to the Executive Branch," three former trade officials warn <a class="Link" href="https://libertyjusticecenter.org/wp-content/uploads/Amicus-Brief-Wolff-Maruyama-Hills.pdf" target="_blank" >in a brief they filed last week</a>. If that sounds familiar, it's because Trump has attempted something similar twice before, only to be rebuffed by the courts.</p><p>This time around, the brief notes, Trump is relying on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, claiming "a sweeping power to impose broad, economywide tariffs untethered from the statute Congress enacted." That assessment is especially noteworthy because the brief's authors, who are urging the Court of International Trade to reject Trump's power grab, were intimately involved in drafting and enforcing Section 301.</p><p>One of them is Alan Wm. Wolff, who directed the Treasury Department's Office of Multilateral Trade Negotiations and served as general counsel for what is now the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative during the Nixon and Ford administrations. Wolff played a leading role in drafting the trade act and wrote the original version of Section 301.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-650000" name="module-650000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Wolff is joined by Carla Hills, the U.S. trade representative under President George H.W. Bush, and Warren Maruyama, who was a U.S. trade representative lawyer during the Reagan administration and the office's general counsel during the George W. Bush administration. Both have extensive experience in implementing Section 301, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/19/2411" target="_blank" >authorizes the trade representative’s office to impose tariffs</a> in response to a foreign "act, policy, or practice" that is "unreasonable or discriminatory' and "burdens or restricts United States commerce."</p><p>Section 301 "was enacted to address specific unfair trade practices by individual U.S. trading partners," Wolff et al. note. But the Trump administration views the provision as a license to impose sweeping tariffs on trading partners that account for nearly all U.S. imports, <a class="Link" href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/july/ustr-takes-action-forced-labor-section-301-investigations" target="_blank" >under the pretext </a>that they have failed to "impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor."</p><p>The upshot of these "often sham 'investigations,'" Wolff et al. note, is a tariff regime strikingly similar to the one Trump tried to impose last year under the <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/50/chapter-35" target="_blank" >International Emergency Economic Powers Act</a>, a 1977 law that does not mention import taxes and had never been used to impose them. In February, after the Supreme Court ruled that the emergency economic powers act does not authorize tariffs at all, Trump switched to Section 122 of the Trade Act, which the international trade court said he had improperly invoked.</p><p>"The Section 301 tariffs appear to be a thinly disguised pretext for reimposing the President's IEEPA tariffs under the guise of dealing with forced labor," Wolff et al. say. As they see it, "nothing in the statute authorizes [the] USTR" to "justify tariffs of unprecedented breadth" by aggregating "dozens of separate investigations" and setting "a novel standard that foreign countries have not in the judgment of the USTR met."</p><p>Contrary to the statute's requirements, the findings underlying that determination do not specify how each of the targets has fallen short or how their supposed failures burden U.S. commerce. Nor has U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer explained why the tariffs can be expected to ameliorate the problem he claims to be addressing.</p><p>The trade act "imposed clear substantive and procedural limits on each tariff authority" it delegated, the brief notes. "It is not at all credible that Congress simultaneously conferred, by implication, an unlimited tariff power through Section 301, administered by a cabinet official, without any indication in the statute or legislative history that it intended to do so."</p><p>By asserting "an effectively boundless Section 301 authority through the aggregation of numerous investigations," Wolff et al. say, Greer "exceeds the limits established by Congress and upsets the constitutional allocation of trade powers." </p><p>But what do they know?</p><p>A thing or two, suggests the Liberty Justice Center, which <a class="Link" href="https://libertyjusticecenter.org/wp-content/uploads/002-Burlap-and-Barrel-v.-Greer-Compl-2026-07-24.pdf" target="_blank" >filed one of the lawsuits challenging Trump’s tariffs</a>.</p><p>"The people who know Section 301 best," it says, "are telling the [international trade court] that the administration is using the statute in a way Congress never designed it to be used."</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fd0000" name="module-fd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

"Another huge influence for us was pirating music with Napster or LimeWire," Jahan added, laughing at the memories.</p><p>Old-school technology is a major theme on Krewella’s latest album "Peak," which abounds with messages about our collective obsession with the proverbial hottest new things and trying to find euphoria in an ever-changing world.</p><p>Grappling with the life twists and thinking about "how things used to be" takes on extra meaning for the now Los Angeles-based sisters as they return home to play Sound-Bar on Saturday.</p><p>"There was a party every single night when we [lived in Chicago]," Yasmine said.
